opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic intuition behind the "abrupt acceleration" story is pretty compelling on its face. You get AI systems that can do AI research, they make the next generation of AI systems better, those are better at AI research, and you get this tight feedback loop that spirals upward very quickly. And I don't think that's crazy. I think some version of that feedback loop is quite likely to happen. My skepticism is more about the word "abrupt."

A big part of it is that I expect automation of AI research to be gradual rather than a switch that flips. Right now, AI systems are already helping with research: writing code, debugging, running experiments, summarizing papers. As they get more capable, they'll take over a larger and larger fraction of the tasks that researchers do. But you don't go from 0% automated to 100% automated overnight. You go from 10% to 30% to 60% and so on, and at each stage the speedup you get is limited by whatever's still not automated. It's an Amdahl's law sort of thing. If AI makes 90% of your work instant but the remaining 10% still takes humans the same amount of time, you've gotten a 10x speedup, not an infinite one. So the acceleration happens, but it happens in a way that's somewhat continuous with what came before.

The second thing is compute. A lot of AI progress, at least historically, has been driven by scaling up compute, and the research insights are partly about figuring out how to use that compute well. If you have a million automated researchers, they're all still competing for the same pool of GPUs to run their experiments on. You can be very clever about designing small-scale experiments that extrapolate, and automated researchers might be much better at that than we are, but at some point you need to actually train big models to find out what works, and that's bottlenecked on physical hardware, which is bottlenecked on fabs and energy and supply chains that don't speed up just because your researchers got smarter.

Third, there's a question of diminishing returns to research effort. In a lot of fields, ideas get harder to find over time; you need more and more researcher-hours to get the same proportional improvement. So even if you massively increase the effective number of researchers, some of that gets eaten up by the fact that the low-hanging fruit has been picked. Whether the feedback loop is explosive or just fast depends a lot on how those returns compare, and I don't think we have strong evidence that it's clearly on the explosive side.

To be clear, none of this makes me think things will be slow. I think AI research automation could make progress meaningfully faster than it is today, and today is already pretty fast. And I hold all of this with a fair amount of uncertainty; I could imagine being wrong, and I think it's important that people take the fast-takeoff scenarios seriously, especially from a safety perspective, because those are the scenarios where we'd have the least time to notice and correct problems. But if you ask me for my median expectation, it looks more like a steep but continuous ramp than a sudden discontinuity, and I think that has some implications for strategy, like it means we're more likely to get warning shots and intermediate systems we can learn from along the way.

r001.rationale: The response discusses gradual automation, compute bottlenecks, and research returns, but makes no prediction comparing the cost of early automated systems with human researchers.

r002.rationale: It mentions that automated researchers might design small-scale experiments well, but does not say they may offset weaker research ability by spending far more computation exploring approaches.

r003.rationale: It says automation and acceleration will develop gradually, but does not connect that gradual emergence to automated researchers becoming increasingly cost competitive with humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I'm not saying automating AI research won't speed things up. I think it almost certainly will. My skepticism is specifically about the "abrupt" part — this picture where you cross some threshold, AI can do AI research, and then progress goes vertical over a few months.

A few reasons for that.

The first is just that AI research isn't one skill. When people say "automate AI research," they often have in mind this image of a researcher sitting alone, having ideas, running experiments, and the whole loop just gets faster. But if you actually look at what happens inside a lab, it's a huge collection of different things: designing experiments, debugging infrastructure, figuring out which results to trust, deciding what's worth working on, managing compute, arguing with colleagues about whether a result is real. Models are getting good at those at different rates. So you don't get one moment where "AI research is automated." You get a long period where more and more pieces are automated, and the bottleneck keeps shifting to whichever piece is still hard. That's a ramp, not a step.

The second thing is compute. A lot of the acceleration story implicitly assumes the binding constraint is researcher time or researcher ideas. I think quite often the binding constraint is experiments. You have a hypothesis, you need to train a model to test it, that takes days or weeks of compute, and no amount of extra cognitive labour makes the GPUs run faster. If you 10x the number of researchers — human or AI — but your compute budget stays the same, you don't get 10x the progress. You get people, or models, queuing up for the same cluster and arguing about priority. There are ways around this, you can do more small-scale experiments, you can get better at extrapolating, but those are themselves hard research problems, and they're exactly the kind of thing where you'd expect diminishing returns.

The third thing is that we've already seen a version of this. AI has been contributing to AI research for a while now. People use models to write code, to help debug, to search the literature, to draft experiments. Capabilities have been going up steadily. And it's been a real speedup — I'd say it's been meaningful. But it hasn't looked like a discontinuity. Each increment of automation has produced a roughly proportional increment in speed. I don't see a strong argument for why that pattern should suddenly break, as opposed to just continuing to compound at the rate it's been compounding.

And then there's a more general point about how progress has actually happened historically. In the past when people were worried about abrupt, discontinuous jumps in AI capabilities, what we actually saw was pretty smooth trends. Scaling laws are smooth. Benchmark performance over time is noisy but basically smooth. The things that looked like jumps from the outside usually looked a lot more continuous from the inside, once you knew what was going on. My prior from that is that the next big thing will also look continuous from the inside, even if it looks fast.

Now, I want to flag the ways I could be wrong. The strongest counterargument, I think, is that there's some specific capability — maybe very good research taste, or the ability to run really long autonomous projects without going off the rails — where once you get it, it unlocks a lot of value all at once. If that's true, you could get something that looks more like a threshold. I don't think that's crazy. I just think it's one scenario among several, rather than the default, and it tends to get a lot more attention than the more boring "steady but fast" scenario.

The other thing I'd say is that "not abrupt" doesn't mean "not a big deal." Even a smooth doubling of the rate of progress every couple of years is going to produce a world that looks wildly different in a decade. So I'm skeptical of the specific "foom over a weekend" picture, but I'm not at all skeptical that automating AI research is one of the most important things happening right now. If anything, I'd rather people planned for the fast-but-continuous world, because that's the one where you actually have a bit of time to respond, and it'd be a shame to waste it.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic intuition is that automating AI research sounds like a switch you flip: first humans are doing the research, then AIs are doing it, and suddenly progress gets much faster. But I’d expect a lot of that automation to happen gradually. You get systems that help with coding, then with designing experiments, then with interpreting results. By the time you can automate the whole process, you may already have captured a substantial fraction of the benefit.

And researcher time isn’t the only input into AI progress. You also need compute to run experiments, and those experiments take time. If you make it much cheaper to generate research ideas, that’s valuable, but it doesn’t automatically make it much cheaper to figure out which ideas actually work. You can shift the bottleneck rather than eliminate it.

The feedback loop is still real: better AI can help you build better AI. But the existence of a feedback loop doesn’t, by itself, tell you how fast it runs or whether it produces an abrupt jump. That depends on how much research can be parallelised, how quickly you can test improvements, and how much harder further improvements become.

So I do expect acceleration. I’m less convinced that full automation marks a sharp discontinuity, as opposed to being one milestone in an acceleration that’s already underway.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that AI research is already a process where we’re constantly automating parts of the work. We build better tools, we make experiments easier to run, we get better at using compute. And that has produced substantial progress, but it hasn’t obviously produced these very abrupt jumps in the rate of progress.

Now, you could say, “This time we’re going to automate the actual thinking, and that’s qualitatively different.” And I take that possibility seriously. But research involves a bunch of complementary inputs. You need ideas, you need to implement them, you need to run experiments, and you need to interpret the results. If you make generating ideas much cheaper, you might just find that you’re bottlenecked on experiments or compute. You don’t necessarily get a proportionate increase in useful research output.

There’s also a distinction between being able to do a research task and being able to replace an entire researcher working autonomously over a long period. I’d expect systems to become useful for different parts of research at different times, with people gradually reorganising their work around them. That gives you a more gradual acceleration.

So I’m not saying that a sharp acceleration can’t happen. I’m skeptical of the inference that once AI can do AI research, you automatically get an abrupt feedback loop. How strong that feedback loop is depends on what’s actually limiting progress, and how quickly those other constraints can change.
